sections.html:
Florissant is a second-ring suburb north of St. Louis and the biggest municipality in its county. Much of its housing went up in the postwar boom, with roughly 18,000 houses built between 1947 and 1980, and that age profile drives what buyers and inspectors ask about. The city covers 12.55 square miles, mostly north of I-270.

Florissant leans toward owners and moderate prices, so a seller here is usually pricing against other mid-century houses on similar lots. About two of every three households own, and 89.6% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier.

sections.h2: Is a city inspection required before selling?
sections.html:
No. A Florissant property can be sold as-is without an inspection, and the buyer then has to obtain and pay for the inspection and the occupancy permit before anyone moves in.

The city built its minimum standards around cooking, heating and sanitary equipment, light and ventilation, and upkeep of existing buildings. Those are the items an inspector walks through. The city's report can differ from a private inspector or an FHA or VA appraisal, and buyers are encouraged to use the results from every source instead of pitting one report against another. If you know the roof, furnace, water heater, electrical panel and plumbing stack all work, the walk-through holds fewer surprises.

  • Public Works and the Building Division handle occupancy permits and inspections.
  • Commercial buildings, including schools and churches, need their own occupancy inspection and permit before use.
  • The Permit Portal at my.florissantmo.com takes business license and commercial occupancy applications.

Florissant's Home Improvement Program offers a no-interest forgivable loan of up to $7,000 for safety and code repairs, secured by a deed of trust. If the owner sells, rents or transfers the home within five years, the loan must be repaid, and for a sale it is paid at closing. Applications are taken in a short window each spring.

If you took a loan in the past five years, call Community Development at 314-839-7680 and get the balance in writing before you sign a contract. Ask your title company whether the deed of trust needs a release at closing.

The Recorder of Deeds charges $26 for page one of a standard deed and $3 for every page after it. A $25 non-standard fee applies if the document does not meet the Missouri Document Formatting Standards, and eRecording vendors may add their own charges. The office is at 41 S Central Ave in Clayton, and originals go by mail or drop-off with a check or money order payable to ROD.

The county Collector of Revenue sends the real estate tax bill. Payment or postmark must land on or before the last day of December. Later payments carry up to 18% interest per year plus a 2% penalty under RSMo chapters 139 and 140. Your title agent can show how the year's bill gets divided at the closing table.

  • Pull a paid-to-date statement from the Collector of Revenue before listing.
  • Ask your title company whether a Home Improvement Program lien needs a release.
  • Request a copy of your recorded deed from the Recorder of Deeds if you cannot find it.

If you think the Assessor valued your house too high, the independent Board of Equalization hears appeals filed between May 1 and the second Monday of July. The Assessor must finalize the rolls by July 1, and after that only the Board can change a value. Keep photos, repair estimates and recent sales for next year's filing.

sections.h2: Which ways of selling fit a Florissant house?
sections.html:
Your route should follow the shape the house is in and the date you need cash. Florissant's older ranch and split-level homes often carry aging mechanical systems, and that shows up in every path below.

  • A listing with an agent reaches the most shoppers. It also brings inspection requests, financing contingencies and the buyer's occupancy inspection.
  • An as-is cash sale suits an owner who would rather skip showings and repairs. The purchaser then takes on the city occupancy process.
  • Selling on your own avoids an agent's fee and keeps pricing, paperwork and negotiation in your hands.

Whichever route you pick, compare the net amount after tax proration, any lien payoff, title charges and deed recording. A higher headline price can leave less in your pocket than a lower offer with fewer conditions. Ask each buyer how long closing takes and whether they pay recording costs.

Because the city does not require a seller inspection, the timeline depends mostly on the buyer. With an as-is sale, the buyer orders the occupancy inspection and pays for it, and any items the inspector flags become the buyer's job. With a listing, expect the buyer's lender to bring its own appraisal and possibly an FHA or VA review, and those reports can disagree with the city's.

Meanwhile you have a short list of your own. Get the paid-to-date tax statement, find out whether a Home Improvement Program lien is attached, and locate your recorded deed. The title agent then divides the year's tax at the table, pays off any lien and sends the deed to Clayton for recording. If you sell for cash, that same sequence runs without the lender's steps, and it can finish in a few weeks.

Florissant is served by two public districts, Hazelwood and Ferguson-Florissant, so the school assignment on a given street matters. McCluer High School and McCluer North High School belong to Ferguson-Florissant, and North Technical High School is also in the city. Hazelwood Northwest Middle School and several elementary schools stand inside city limits.

Old Town draws a different buyer. It is a locally designated historic district, created by ordinance in 1969, and the St. Ferdinand Central Historic District there carries a National Register listing. It holds Missouri German brick buildings such as the Kuehn House, French wood-frame homes and the Old St. Ferdinand Shrine. The wider resource area covers about 156 city blocks and 124 historically significant properties built between 1790 and 1940. If your house sits inside those blocks, ask the city whether exterior changes need review before you make repairs.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Florissant house without a city inspection?
faqs.a: Yes. The city lets a house sell as-is. Whoever buys it must obtain the inspection and occupancy permit before anyone moves in, which puts that step on the buyer's timeline.

faqs.q: Who records the deed after a Florissant sale?
faqs.a: The St. Louis County Recorder of Deeds, at 41 S Central Ave in Clayton. A standard deed costs $26 for the first page and $3 for each added page, plus $25 if the format is non-standard.

faqs.q: When does the county want Florissant property tax paid?
faqs.a: By December 31, either paid or postmarked that day. Anything later adds up to 18% interest per year and a 2% penalty under RSMo 139 and 140.

faqs.q: What happens to a Home Improvement Program loan if I sell?
faqs.a: It comes due. A sale within five years of the loan date requires repayment, and for a sale the loan is repaid at closing. Call 314-839-7680 for the balance.
Federal estimates put the city at 51,124 residents in mid-2025, 2.7% below the 52,537 used as the 2020 base. The 1970 census counted 65,908.
